answers.answer: Embedded means the SQLite engine runs inside the application process: code calls it directly to execute SQL, rather than crossing a network boundary to a separate database server. Persistent data lives in a local file; in-memory databases are also supported. It retains relational tables, joins, indexes and transactions. Application-local data benefits from direct access and fewer services, including offline use. Many application servers updating shared data over a network introduce locality, shared-access and competing-write requirements; a client/server database is often a better fit. SQLite can still serve web users through an application server using local storage. User count and size alone do not describe write contention, transaction duration or where access occurs; verify those requirements instead. Independent files do not synchronize automatically: additional software and conflict handling are required.

evidence.quote: The engine runs inside your application's process. Your code calls SQLite directly, rather than sending queries to a separate database server.
Here, this means there is no separate database server to manage. A persistent database lives in a local file. SQLite also supports in-memory databases.
SQLite stores data in tables and supports SQL queries, joins, indexes, and transactions.
SQLite can also sit behind a web application. Users contact the application server, which accesses its local database.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns. SQLite can still be suitable behind an application server with local storage.
Sharing changes between independent device or server copies requires additional software. Local transactions do not resolve conflicting edits elsewhere.

answers.answer: Affinity guides conversions in ordinary tables, while each value has its own storage class; an integer column can retain unconvertible text. STRICT tables enforce declared types after permitted conversions, except ANY. Primary keys identify rows, UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values, CHECK rejects false conditions, and foreign keys constrain references to existing rows. Required values need explicit NOT NULL: CHECK alone does not establish that missing values are invalid, and foreign-key references may be null. Before transactions, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection and query PRAGMA foreign_keys to verify 1. Atomicity means all grouped changes succeed or none take effect; consistency preserves defined rules; isolation controls visibility and write coordination, normally hiding incomplete changes; durability preserves commits according to configuration and storage guarantees. Commit accepts the group and rollback cancels its database work. Constraints define the rules and correct transaction logic remains necessary because isolation does not eliminate application races or lock waits. Journaling provides recovery state; durability also depends on flushing settings, reliable filesystem locking and storage honoring flush requests. Delayed flushing can lose recent commits after power failure. Rollback cannot reverse an external network side effect because it covers only database work in the transaction.

evidence.quote: Ordinary tables use affinity to guide conversions; each value has a storage class, such as integer, text or null. A declared integer column can retain text that cannot be converted.
These enforce stronger type checks. Values must fit the declared type after permitted conversions, except columns explicitly declared ANY.
Primary keys identify rows; UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values and CHECK rejects false conditions. Combine CHECK with NOT NULL when a missing value must also be invalid.

Constrain references to existing rows; null references are allowed unless separately forbidden. Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
Groups database changes. Commit accepts them; rollback cancels them.
All changes succeed together, or none take effect.
Changes preserve the rules you defined.
Controls concurrent visibility and write coordination. Normal settings hide incomplete changes, but do not remove application races, lock waits or the need for correct transaction logic.
Committed changes survive failures according to the configured guarantees. This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.
Durability settings can trade crash protection for speed. Settings that delay flushing committed changes to persistent storage can lose recent transactions after a power failure.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change. In this mode, readers and writers can block each other.
Only database work inside the transaction is covered. Rollback does not reverse an external network side effect.

answers.answer: Several connections, including different processes on one machine, may exist, but only one can actively write each database at a time. Write contention is competing demand for that required write access; SQLITE_BUSY means a connection cannot obtain required access. Short transactions reduce the time other writes wait, especially by avoiding network waits inside them. Busy timeouts or bounded retries can tolerate brief contention; failed attempts must be handled, sometimes by retrying the transaction. Waiting does not add writer capacity or guarantee success. Rollback journaling records original data to undo interrupted changes, and readers and writers may block each other. WAL records changes in a separate log so readers retain stable snapshots while a writer commits. Checkpointing transfers logged changes to the main database file. Long reads can delay this transfer and grow the log. WAL still has one writer and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine; do not infer that a network-shared file supports a multi-host WAL deployment. Reliable filesystem locking and storage flush behavior also matter. The lesson does not provide a general shared-filesystem validation procedure.

evidence.quote: SQLite supports multiple connections, including connections from different processes on the same machine. But each database allows only one active writer at a time.

A connection can receive this result when it cannot obtain required access. A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention; some failures require retrying the transaction. Waiting does not create another writer or guarantee success.
Keep write transactions short. A transaction that waits on a network request can hold up unrelated writes.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change. In this mode, readers and writers can block each other.
Records changes in a separate log. Readers can continue using a stable snapshot while a writer commits changes.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.
Committed changes survive failures according to the configured guarantees. This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.

answers.answer: An index is an additional structure that can avoid scanning or sorting every row. A query plan is the chosen access and processing steps for filtering, joins, sorting and aggregation. For the stated owner filter and time ordering, a composite index ordered by owner then time is a candidate inferred from matching columns to the filter and requested ordering; it is not a guaranteed optimal plan. Inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for the chosen access and processing steps and measure representative queries. The lesson supplies no actual plan output or precise syntax for this candidate. Scans may be preferable for small tables or broad queries, and an existing index need not be chosen. Indexes consume space and require write maintenance; local execution still costs CPU, I/O and memory. Operations still include access permissions, capacity/free space, recovery and coordinated schema migrations across application versions and active access; some migrations rebuild and copy tables. Backups must preserve consistent active database state: copying only the main file can omit committed data still in WAL. Use a supported consistent backup method, retain backups for recovery needs and test restoration and application usability. A verified quiescent state would need evidence that required state is captured consistently; the lesson does not provide a quiescence procedure or establish that simply stopping writes makes a main-file copy safe. A file alone proves neither consistency nor recovery time.

evidence.quote: Chooses access and processing steps for joins, filtering, sorting and aggregation. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows those steps.
An additional structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows. Match columns and their order to actual filters and requested ordering; a composite index contains multiple columns.
A scan can be preferable for small tables or broad queries. The planner need not use an index merely because it exists. Measure representative queries.
Local execution still uses CPU, storage I/O and memory. Indexes take space and add write maintenance; avoiding a network call does not make expensive work free.
A migration changes stored structure. Coordinate it with application versions and active access; some changes require rebuilding a table and copying data.
Use a supported consistent backup method for an active database. Committed data may still be in the WAL, so copying only the main file can omit required state.
Manage access permissions and free space. Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability. A backup file alone does not prove consistency or recovery time.

answers.answer: SQLite is a plausible choice for the single-host application: local access reduces services and short occasional writes can take turns. Multiple connections are allowed; WAL can improve reader/writer overlap on that host, but still permits only one writer. For several servers making sustained concurrent writes to shared data, favor a client/server database if those writes cannot take turns: WAL neither adds writers nor supports its shared-memory design across machines. Separate SQLite copies would require additional synchronization and conflict handling. In either design, define types and constraints, verify foreign-key enforcement on each SQLite connection, use correct transaction logic, inspect and measure representative query plans and choose indexes with write cost in mind. SQLite also needs consistent backups, restore tests and coordinated migrations. Before committing, verify data locality and access topology, write contention and transaction duration, burst/sustained competing work, busy failures and acceptable waiting, representative query behavior, read duration/checkpoint progress and WAL growth, storage capacity and locking/flush guarantees, required data rules, synchronization/conflict requirements, failure tolerance and recovery time. These are measurements or requirements to establish, not evidence already supplied; no throughput threshold or benchmark is provided by the lesson.
